competency_name: Browsing, searching and filtering data, information and digital content
plain_language_summary: Finding reliable information online by knowing where to look, how to search effectively, and how to filter out noise and low-quality sources.
why_it_matters_in_he: Academic work depends on locating authoritative evidence quickly. Poor search strategy wastes time and produces weaker arguments. AI-generated summaries have made it even harder to distinguish primary evidence from derivative content.

basic.plain_description: Uses standard search engines and follows given links. Knows that not all sources are equal but relies mainly on what appears first.
basic.common_misread: Assumes someone who can Google is already competent at this level.
basic.example_in_he: A first-year student searches Google Scholar for an essay topic and uses the first three results.

intermediate.plain_description: Uses advanced search operators, discipline-specific databases, and filters by date or peer-review status. Can explain why one source is preferable to another.
intermediate.common_misread: Assumes database access equals search skill.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer refines a literature search using Boolean operators in Scopus and filters by open access.

advanced.plain_description: Designs systematic search strategies, documents search decisions, and critiques the limitations of any search approach. Evaluates AI-assisted search tools critically.
advanced.common_misread: Confuses breadth of searching with depth of evaluation.
advanced.example_in_he: A researcher constructs a reproducible search protocol for a systematic review, including search terms, databases, and exclusion criteria.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops or evaluates new approaches to information discovery. Advises others on search methodology and contributes to institutional knowledge practices.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates technical expertise with the ability to teach or lead others.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: An information specialist designs faculty-wide search skills training and evaluates AI tools for literature discovery.

he_role_notes.educator: Needs to model good search practice and design assessments that reward source quality over source volume.
he_role_notes.student: Often overestimates their own competence here. Training in database searching has measurable impact on assessment quality.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Library and research support staff operate at advanced or highly advanced level; administrative staff often at basic.
he_role_notes.researcher: Systematic review methodology requires advanced level as a baseline.

ai_framing: AI search tools (Perplexity, Copilot, Elicit) change the workflow but not the need to evaluate sources critically. A basic user may trust AI summaries uncritically; an advanced user interrogates provenance.

competency_name: Evaluating data, information and digital content
plain_language_summary: Judging whether information is trustworthy, accurate, current, and appropriate for a given purpose.
why_it_matters_in_he: Academic integrity and research quality depend on rigorous source evaluation. The proliferation of AI-generated content has raised the stakes considerably.

basic.plain_description: Applies simple checklists (author, date, publisher) to evaluate sources. Recognises obviously unreliable content.
basic.common_misread: Assumes anyone who has heard of CRAAP or SIFT is operating at this level.
basic.example_in_he: A student checks whether a website has an author and a publication date before citing it.

intermediate.plain_description: Triangulates across multiple sources, distinguishes primary from secondary evidence, and identifies bias or conflicts of interest.
intermediate.common_misread: Assumes volume of sources cited indicates quality of evaluation.
intermediate.example_in_he: A postgraduate student compares two conflicting meta-analyses and identifies methodological reasons for the discrepancy.

advanced.plain_description: Systematically evaluates evidence quality using domain-specific standards. Critically appraises AI-generated content and statistical claims.
advanced.common_misread: Confuses disciplinary expertise with transferable evaluation skill.
advanced.example_in_he: A lecturer uses critical appraisal tools to assess RCT quality and teaches students to do the same.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops evaluation frameworks or tools for institutional or disciplinary use. Leads training in critical evaluation for staff and students.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Assumes senior academics automatically operate here.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A digital literacy lead develops an AI content verification protocol adopted across a faculty.

he_role_notes.educator: Evaluation competence should be made explicit in module design rather than assumed.
he_role_notes.student: Lateral reading and fact-checking habits are teachable and have strong assessment impact.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Communications and marketing staff especially need intermediate-level evaluation skills for external content.
he_role_notes.researcher: Advanced evaluation is a professional baseline; highly advanced may involve contributing to methodology literature.

ai_framing: AI can generate convincing but inaccurate content. Evaluating AI output requires the same rigour as evaluating any other source, plus awareness of hallucination and training data bias.

competency_name: Managing data, information and digital content
plain_language_summary: Organising, storing, protecting, and sharing digital files and data in ways that support retrieval, collaboration, and long-term use.
why_it_matters_in_he: Research reproducibility, GDPR compliance, and collaborative working all depend on sound data management. Poor practice leads to lost work, security incidents, and failed audits.

basic.plain_description: Saves files in named folders and uses basic cloud storage. Understands why backing up matters.
basic.common_misread: Assumes anyone using OneDrive or Google Drive is managing data well.
basic.example_in_he: A student saves lecture notes in a folder structure by module and syncs to cloud storage.

intermediate.plain_description: Uses consistent naming conventions, version control, and access permissions. Understands basic data retention rules.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses storage capacity with data management maturity.
intermediate.example_in_he: A professional services administrator applies a file naming protocol across a shared team drive and sets appropriate sharing permissions.

advanced.plain_description: Implements a data management plan, applies FAIR principles, and manages research data across its full lifecycle including archiving and disposal.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes DMP completion equals genuine data management competence.
advanced.example_in_he: A researcher deposits data in an institutional repository with appropriate metadata and licencing for open access compliance.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Designs data management infrastructure or policy at institutional or disciplinary level. Advises on standards and leads community practice.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates technical systems knowledge with governance expertise.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A research data manager develops an institution-wide data management policy aligned to funder requirements and GDPR.

he_role_notes.educator: Needs to model good practice and brief students on requirements at the start of research projects.
he_role_notes.student: Often unaware of institutional expectations; direct instruction at onboarding is effective.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Research support and administrative staff often need intermediate level as a job requirement.
he_role_notes.researcher: Advanced level is expected for funded research; highly advanced for those designing data infrastructure.

ai_framing: AI tools that process or store data (e.g. prompting with personal or research data) raise new data management questions around consent, retention, and ownership.

plain_language_summary: Using digital tools to communicate with others appropriately, choosing the right channel for the right purpose and audience.
why_it_matters_in_he: Students, staff, and researchers work across multiple platforms (email, Teams, VLEs, social media). Choosing the wrong channel or tone has real professional consequences.

basic.plain_description: Uses email and common messaging tools. Aware that different tools have different purposes.
basic.common_misread: Assumes digital natives are automatically competent communicators online.
basic.example_in_he: A student emails their tutor to request an extension using an appropriate subject line and professional tone.

intermediate.plain_description: Adapts communication style and channel to context and audience. Uses collaborative platforms (Teams, Slack, VLE discussion boards) effectively.
intermediate.common_misread: Conflates frequency of use with quality of communication.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer coordinates a group project using a structured Teams channel with clear conventions for different types of communication.

advanced.plain_description: Manages complex multi-stakeholder communications across multiple platforms. Designs communication frameworks for teams or cohorts.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes project management experience equals communication design skill.
advanced.example_in_he: A programme director designs a communication plan for a new curriculum, specifying channels, audiences, and frequency.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional standards or tools for digital communication. Leads communities of practice around digital engagement.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates seniority with communication design expertise.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A digital communications lead develops institutional guidelines for staff use of professional social media.

he_role_notes.educator: Models professional digital communication and sets expectations explicitly for student interactions.
he_role_notes.student: May need explicit guidance on professional tone in academic contexts; peer norms often differ from institutional expectations.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Often the primary interface between institution and external stakeholders; intermediate level is a baseline.
he_role_notes.researcher: Increasingly expected to communicate research through public-facing digital channels.

ai_framing: AI writing tools can assist with drafting communications but may homogenise tone or miss contextual nuance. Critical review of AI-drafted messages is part of intermediate-level competence.

plain_language_summary: Sharing files, data, and knowledge with others through digital means while respecting copyright, privacy, and access rights.
why_it_matters_in_he: Open access, research dissemination, and collaborative working all require confident, ethical sharing practices. Sharing personal or restricted data carelessly causes real harm.

basic.plain_description: Can share files and links. Understands that some content cannot be freely shared.
basic.common_misread: Assumes willingness to share equals competence in sharing appropriately.
basic.example_in_he: A student shares a group project document via a VLE submission link rather than a personal email attachment.

intermediate.plain_description: Applies appropriate licences and access settings. Understands Creative Commons and basic copyright. Shares responsibly in professional contexts.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses open access with absence of attribution requirements.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer shares lecture recordings with their cohort using time-limited access links and removes them after the module ends.

advanced.plain_description: Designs sharing workflows for teams or projects. Applies open licencing strategically and advises others on intellectual property.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes knowledge of licencing types equals ability to apply them correctly in context.
advanced.example_in_he: A researcher publishes a dataset under a CC BY licence and documents provenance and access conditions for reuse.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional sharing policy or open access infrastructure. Leads practice across departments or disciplines.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates policy authorship with operational competence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A scholarly communications librarian develops a university-wide open access policy and supports compliance across faculties.

he_role_notes.educator: Needs to model appropriate sharing of learning materials and discuss intellectual property with students.
he_role_notes.student: Often unclear about what they can legally share; explicit guidance at module level is effective.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Communications and IT staff often manage sharing infrastructure.
he_role_notes.researcher: Open access mandates from funders make advanced sharing competence increasingly non-optional.

ai_framing: Sharing prompts or outputs from AI tools raises questions about ownership and attribution that are not yet fully resolved in HE policy.

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
plain_language_summary: Participating in digital public life responsibly, contributing to online communities, and understanding how digital engagement shapes civic outcomes.
why_it_matters_in_he: Universities are civic institutions. Staff and students represent them online. Digital civic engagement also connects to research impact, public engagement, and student employability.

basic.plain_description: Participates in online communities. Aware that online behaviour has real consequences.
basic.common_misread: Assumes social media usage equals civic digital competence.
basic.example_in_he: A student participates in a module discussion board and understands the code of conduct that applies.

intermediate.plain_description: Engages constructively in digital civic spaces. Understands how algorithms shape what content is visible and why this matters.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses online activism with civic competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer contributes to a professional network discussion with evidence-based arguments and cites sources.

advanced.plain_description: Uses digital platforms strategically for public engagement or advocacy. Critically analyses the role of digital technologies in democratic processes.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes public engagement experience equals advanced competence.
advanced.example_in_he: A researcher uses social media to disseminate findings to non-specialist audiences and engages with responses critically.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Leads digital civic initiatives or contributes to policy on digital participation. Develops frameworks for responsible digital engagement in institutional or public contexts.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates institutional seniority with civic digital leadership.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A digital strategy lead develops guidance on university social media engagement during public debates, balancing academic freedom and institutional reputation.

he_role_notes.educator: Academic freedom intersects with civic digital engagement; clear institutional guidance helps staff navigate this.
he_role_notes.student: Student union and representation activities often provide civic digital engagement contexts.
he_role_notes.professional_services: External communications roles carry highest exposure; clear escalation protocols matter.
he_role_notes.researcher: Public engagement outputs increasingly assessed in REF impact cases.

ai_framing: AI-generated content in civic spaces (deepfakes, synthetic media, AI personas) is an emerging threat to informed participation that HE professionals should understand and be able to explain.

plain_language_summary: Working effectively with others using digital tools, from co-authoring documents to managing shared projects across teams and time zones.
why_it_matters_in_he: Research, curriculum development, and professional services all involve collaborative digital work. Ineffective digital collaboration wastes time and produces weaker outputs.

basic.plain_description: Can share and edit documents with others. Uses basic collaboration features in common tools.
basic.common_misread: Assumes simultaneous document access equals effective collaboration.
basic.example_in_he: A student contributes to a shared Google Doc for a group presentation.

intermediate.plain_description: Uses collaborative platforms (Teams, SharePoint, Miro) effectively. Establishes shared conventions and contributes to productive group workflows.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses tool access with collaboration competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A project team uses a shared task board, agreed naming conventions, and asynchronous review comments to co-author a report.

advanced.plain_description: Designs and manages collaborative digital workflows for complex projects. Supports others in using collaborative tools effectively.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes project management certification implies digital collaboration expertise.
advanced.example_in_he: A research PI sets up a collaborative workspace for a multi-institution project with defined roles, version control, and documentation standards.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional frameworks or tools for digital collaboration. Leads cross-organisational collaboration initiatives.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates platform administration with strategic collaboration leadership.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A digital workplace lead designs a university-wide collaboration framework that integrates Microsoft 365, VLE, and research platforms.

he_role_notes.educator: Group assessment design should account for varied student collaboration competence rather than assuming it.
he_role_notes.student: Asynchronous collaboration skills are underdeveloped in many students; they benefit from explicit scaffolding.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Cross-department projects require intermediate-level collaboration competence as a baseline.
he_role_notes.researcher: International and interdisciplinary research increasingly depends on advanced collaboration tool competence.

ai_framing: AI co-pilots embedded in collaboration tools (Copilot in Teams/Word) change workflows. Understanding what AI is doing to shared documents -- summarising, drafting, suggesting -- is part of advanced collaboration competence.

plain_language_summary: Understanding and applying appropriate behavioural norms in online environments, including being respectful, professional, and aware of the impact of digital communication.
why_it_matters_in_he: Online incivility in HE damages learning environments, erodes trust, and can have disciplinary consequences. As more teaching and professional interaction moves online, netiquette matters more.

basic.plain_description: Behaves respectfully online and understands basic rules of digital etiquette.
basic.common_misread: Assumes rule-following equals genuine understanding of impact.
basic.example_in_he: A student reads and complies with the VLE discussion board guidelines.

intermediate.plain_description: Adapts tone and register across different digital contexts. Recognises and responds constructively to poor netiquette by others.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses politeness with genuine netiquette competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A tutor models constructive online feedback in a discussion thread and redirects an off-topic or heated exchange.

advanced.plain_description: Designs online learning or professional environments with netiquette expectations built in. Supports others in developing their practice.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes good personal practice transfers automatically to designing environments for others.
advanced.example_in_he: A module lead co-designs community agreements with students at the start of an online module and addresses breaches constructively.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional netiquette policy or training. Leads culture change around digital communication norms.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates policy drafting with genuine cultural influence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: An EDI lead develops training on inclusive online communication for all staff and embeds it in induction.

he_role_notes.educator: Explicit norm-setting at module start reduces later problems; reactive moderation alone is insufficient.
he_role_notes.student: Students often carry consumer-internet norms into academic spaces; explicit induction content helps.
he_role_notes.professional_services: External-facing roles require clear guidance on professional digital communication standards.
he_role_notes.researcher: Online academic debate (social media, blogs, pre-print commenting) requires both competence and institutional guidance.

ai_framing: AI-generated communications can lack appropriate context or sensitivity. Users who deploy AI-drafted messages without critical review may inadvertently violate netiquette norms.

plain_language_summary: Consciously shaping and managing your online presence and reputation across different digital platforms and professional contexts.
why_it_matters_in_he: Staff, students, and researchers all have digital footprints that affect professional opportunities. Unmanaged digital identities create risk; well-managed ones create advantage.

basic.plain_description: Aware of having a digital presence and that others can search for it.
basic.common_misread: Assumes having a LinkedIn profile equals managing digital identity.
basic.example_in_he: A student sets their social media accounts to private before applying for graduate roles.

intermediate.plain_description: Actively curates professional digital presence. Manages privacy settings strategically and is consistent across platforms.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses a polished profile with a managed identity strategy.
intermediate.example_in_he: A postgraduate student maintains an academic profile (ORCID, institutional page) that accurately represents their work.

advanced.plain_description: Builds and maintains a coherent professional digital identity strategy. Advises others on managing their online presence in professional contexts.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes high follower counts or engagement metrics indicate advanced identity management.
advanced.example_in_he: A lecturer develops a public-facing academic profile including a research blog, social media, and institutional page, with a consistent narrative across platforms.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional frameworks or guidance for digital identity management. Leads training for staff and students.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates personal competence with the ability to design programmes for others.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A careers service lead develops a digital identity curriculum embedded in all undergraduate programmes.

he_role_notes.educator: Academic identity online (ORCID, ResearchGate, institutional page) affects research visibility and citation.
he_role_notes.student: Digital identity management is a graduate employability skill that benefits from early, explicit development.
he_role_notes.professional_services: External-facing roles require especially careful management of the boundary between personal and professional identity.
he_role_notes.researcher: Open research and public engagement expectations are increasing the professional importance of a managed online research identity.

ai_framing: AI-generated content attributed to a person (e.g. AI-assisted blog posts, auto-generated bios) raises questions of authenticity and attribution in professional digital identity contexts.

plain_language_summary: Creating digital materials -- documents, presentations, images, video, audio -- that are fit for purpose, accessible, and well-designed.
why_it_matters_in_he: Teaching materials, research outputs, and professional communications all involve creating digital content. Poor content creation competence produces materials that are hard to use, inaccessible, or unconvincing.

basic.plain_description: Creates basic documents and presentations using common tools. Content is functional but may lack structure or accessibility.
basic.common_misread: Assumes anyone who can open Word or PowerPoint operates at this level.
basic.example_in_he: A student submits an essay in Word with headings and a reference list.

intermediate.plain_description: Creates structured, accessible, and purposeful digital content across multiple formats. Uses templates and style guides appropriately.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses aesthetic polish with accessibility or purpose-fitness.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer creates a structured VLE page with accessible headings, alt-text on images, and clear navigation.

advanced.plain_description: Designs content for diverse audiences and platforms. Applies accessibility standards, branding guidelines, and instructional design principles.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes content creation tool expertise equals design competence.
advanced.example_in_he: An educational developer designs an online module using WCAG accessibility guidelines, inclusive design principles, and multimedia learning theory.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Leads institutional content creation standards or develops training for others. Innovates in content formats or production approaches.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates creative output with the ability to establish institutional standards.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A digital learning lead develops an institution-wide content creation policy, including accessibility standards, branding, and quality assurance processes.

he_role_notes.educator: Teaching content quality has direct impact on student experience and learning outcomes. Accessibility is a legal obligation.
he_role_notes.student: Multimodal content creation is an employability skill increasingly expected across disciplines.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Communications staff operate at advanced level; general administrative staff at basic/intermediate.
he_role_notes.researcher: Open research and public engagement outputs require content creation competence beyond traditional academic writing.

ai_framing: Generative AI significantly changes content creation workflows. Using AI tools effectively -- prompting, reviewing, editing -- is now part of intermediate-level content creation competence.

plain_language_summary: Combining, adapting, and transforming existing digital content to create something new, while respecting intellectual property rights.
why_it_matters_in_he: Research synthesis, curriculum design, and many professional tasks involve remixing and repurposing content. Doing this without understanding IPR creates legal and reputational risk.

basic.plain_description: Can combine content from different sources. Aware that repurposing others' work requires permission or attribution.
basic.common_misread: Assumes copy-paste with attribution equals legitimate content integration.
basic.example_in_he: A student incorporates a Creative Commons image into a presentation and provides attribution.

intermediate.plain_description: Adapts and transforms content from multiple sources into coherent outputs. Applies relevant licences and fair dealing provisions correctly.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses transformative use with any modification of original content.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer adapts OER materials from multiple sources into a cohesive learning resource and documents the licences applied.

advanced.plain_description: Designs workflows for content integration at scale. Advises on intellectual property in complex cases including AI-generated content.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes legal knowledge is required for advanced competence in this area.
advanced.example_in_he: A curriculum designer builds a process for sourcing, adapting, and licencing OER content across a programme redesign.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional policy on content repurposing and IP. Contributes to sector-level guidance on emerging issues including AI-generated content.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates legal expertise with digital content integration competence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A scholarly communications expert contributes to sector guidance on the intellectual property status of AI-generated academic outputs.

he_role_notes.educator: OER adoption and remixing is central to sustainable curriculum design; competence here reduces time and cost.
he_role_notes.student: Understanding transformative use and plagiarism boundaries is increasingly important as AI tools change writing practices.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Marketing and communications staff regularly repurpose content and need intermediate-level IP understanding.
he_role_notes.researcher: Data and content derived from AI tools sit in an evolving IP landscape that requires active navigation.

ai_framing: AI-generated content has uncertain IP status in most jurisdictions. Understanding the provenance of AI output -- including training data -- is part of advanced competence in this area.

plain_language_summary: Understanding how copyright and licencing work in digital contexts, including when and how you can use, share, and adapt others' work.
why_it_matters_in_he: Copyright infringement creates legal and reputational risk for individuals and institutions. Open licencing supports research impact and educational reach.

basic.plain_description: Knows that copyright exists and that not all digital content is free to use.
basic.common_misread: Assumes finding something online means it is free to use.
basic.example_in_he: A student uses only images labelled for reuse in a presentation.

intermediate.plain_description: Applies Creative Commons licences and understands fair dealing exceptions. Correctly attributes content from different licence types.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses attribution with permission.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer checks the licence on journal articles before uploading to a VLE and uses the library's digital resource system for restricted content.

advanced.plain_description: Advises on copyright in complex cases. Designs licencing strategies for institutional or research outputs. Understands the implications of AI training data.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes legal training is needed for advanced competence.
advanced.example_in_he: A research lead selects appropriate open licences for a project's outputs and advises team members on third-party rights clearance.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional IP or copyright policy. Contributes to sector or policy-level discussions on copyright in digital and AI contexts.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates policy authorship with strategic IP competence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A legal and compliance officer develops institutional guidance on copyright in AI-assisted research and teaching.

he_role_notes.educator: Copyright compliance in learning materials is both a legal obligation and a professional responsibility.
he_role_notes.student: Confusion about copyright is common; targeted, contextual guidance at point of need is more effective than standalone training.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Procurement, communications, and IT staff each face distinct copyright questions.
he_role_notes.researcher: Open access mandates require active engagement with licencing choices.

ai_framing: AI systems trained on copyrighted content, and the outputs they produce, sit in contested legal territory. HE professionals need awareness of this even if they cannot resolve the legal questions themselves.

plain_language_summary: Writing, understanding, and adapting code and computational logic to automate tasks, analyse data, or build digital tools.
why_it_matters_in_he: Data-driven research, learning analytics, and digital innovation increasingly require coding skills. Even non-programmers benefit from understanding what code does and how to work with those who write it.

basic.plain_description: Has a conceptual understanding of what programming is and can run or adapt simple scripts with guidance.
basic.common_misread: Assumes anyone who has run a Python notebook is a programmer.
basic.example_in_he: A social science student runs a provided R script to generate summary statistics from survey data.

intermediate.plain_description: Writes functional code in at least one language to solve defined problems. Can read and adapt others' code and uses version control.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses completing online courses with working programming competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A researcher writes Python scripts to clean and merge datasets and stores code in a Git repository.

advanced.plain_description: Writes well-structured, documented, reusable code. Designs software solutions for research or professional tasks. Reviews and improves others' code.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes experience in one language equals advanced competence broadly.
advanced.example_in_he: A data scientist develops a reusable analysis pipeline with tests and documentation, shared as an open-source library.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Leads software development initiatives or computational research programmes. Contributes to standards or tools used by the broader community.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates technical expertise with the ability to lead or teach others.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A research software engineer leads an RSE team, designs architecture for a university-wide data platform, and contributes to national HPC software projects.

he_role_notes.educator: Computational thinking is increasingly a graduate attribute across disciplines; educators need sufficient understanding to support students even without full programming competence.
he_role_notes.student: Basic data literacy and scripting skills are increasingly expected in research-active disciplines.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Data, analytics, and systems roles require intermediate-to-advanced programming competence.
he_role_notes.researcher: Research reproducibility and open science norms are raising the expected baseline for coding in research.

ai_framing: AI coding assistants (Copilot, Cursor, Claude) fundamentally change how code is written. Using them effectively -- understanding output, debugging, maintaining code quality -- is now part of intermediate programming competence.

plain_language_summary: Keeping your digital devices secure through good hygiene practices like updates, passwords, and antivirus protection.
why_it_matters_in_he: Device compromise is a major route for data breaches, ransomware, and credential theft. Individual device hygiene is a critical layer of institutional security.

basic.plain_description: Keeps devices updated, uses a password, and avoids obviously risky behaviour.
basic.common_misread: Assumes owning a university-managed device means personal security competence.
basic.example_in_he: A student enables automatic updates and uses a strong unique password on their personal laptop.

intermediate.plain_description: Uses MFA, understands VPN, encrypts sensitive data, and manages device risk across personal and work devices.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses following IT policy with actively managing device security.
intermediate.example_in_he: A staff member uses MFA on all work accounts, connects via VPN when working remotely, and encrypts a USB drive containing student data.

advanced.plain_description: Advises others on device security. Identifies and responds to security incidents. Understands device threat models in specific HE contexts.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes IT support experience equals security competence.
advanced.example_in_he: An IT administrator conducts a device security audit, identifies non-compliant endpoints, and implements a remediation plan.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Designs institutional device security policy and infrastructure. Leads security incident response.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates technical depth with strategic security leadership.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A CISO develops an endpoint security strategy aligned to Cyber Essentials Plus and GDPR requirements.

he_role_notes.educator: Often work across personal and institutional devices; clear policy and support for this context matters.
he_role_notes.student: Personal device security is often low; targeted guidance at enrolment and for research students handling sensitive data is effective.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Data-handling roles require at minimum intermediate device security competence.
he_role_notes.researcher: Fieldwork and international travel create specific device security risks that require targeted guidance.

ai_framing: AI assistant apps may request device permissions or access to files. Understanding what access is being granted and to whom is part of intermediate device security competence.

plain_language_summary: Understanding how personal data is collected, used, and shared online, and taking steps to protect your own and others' privacy.
why_it_matters_in_he: GDPR creates legal obligations for anyone handling personal data. Students and staff also have personal privacy interests that digital systems can undermine if not managed carefully.

basic.plain_description: Understands that personal data is collected online and takes basic steps to protect their own privacy.
basic.common_misread: Assumes clicking 'reject all cookies' equals privacy competence.
basic.example_in_he: A student reviews the privacy settings on their university online accounts during induction.

intermediate.plain_description: Understands GDPR rights and obligations at a working level. Manages privacy settings purposefully and handles others' personal data responsibly.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses completing a GDPR awareness module with operational data privacy competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A professional services administrator processes student data using the correct lawful basis, applies data minimisation, and correctly handles a subject access request.

advanced.plain_description: Applies privacy by design principles, conducts DPIAs, and advises on data privacy in project or research contexts.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes legal knowledge is the primary component of advanced privacy competence.
advanced.example_in_he: A researcher completes a DPIA for a project involving sensitive personal data, identifies risks, and implements mitigations before data collection begins.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional data protection policy and practice. Leads GDPR compliance programmes and responds to regulatory challenges.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates DPO role with highly advanced individual competence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A Data Protection Officer develops and implements an institution-wide data protection framework, manages ICO engagement, and leads staff training.

he_role_notes.educator: Research and teaching involving personal data require at minimum intermediate competence and awareness of when to seek specialist advice.
he_role_notes.student: GDPR awareness relevant at basic level; research students handling personal data need intermediate guidance.
he_role_notes.professional_services: HR, finance, and student services roles require intermediate competence as a job baseline.
he_role_notes.researcher: Research ethics and data protection intersect; advanced competence required for studies involving personal data.

ai_framing: Prompting AI tools with personal data raises GDPR questions about data processing, lawful basis, and third-party data transfers. This is now a practical privacy issue for all HE staff.

plain_language_summary: Being aware of and managing the physical, mental, and social risks that come with digital technology use, while also recognising the benefits.
why_it_matters_in_he: Digital intensity in HE work and study creates real wellbeing risks including screen fatigue, always-on culture, and social media effects on self-image, especially for students.

basic.plain_description: Aware of basic digital health risks and takes some steps to manage them.
basic.common_misread: Assumes awareness equals behaviour change.
basic.example_in_he: A student sets a study timer and takes regular screen breaks during revision.

intermediate.plain_description: Actively manages digital wellbeing for themselves and is aware of the impact of digital environments on others.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses productivity tools with wellbeing management.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer sets a clear email response window policy, disables out-of-hours notifications, and models healthy digital boundaries with their team.

advanced.plain_description: Designs digital work or learning environments with wellbeing considerations built in. Supports others in managing digital health.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes personal wellbeing practice transfers to designing environments for others.
advanced.example_in_he: A module leader redesigns an online module to reduce cognitive load, add explicit rest points, and include guidance on managing digital overwhelm.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional digital wellbeing policy or strategy. Leads research or practice in digital health in educational or workplace contexts.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates HR welfare expertise with digital wellbeing strategy.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A wellbeing director develops an institution-wide digital wellbeing framework covering students and staff, grounded in current evidence.

he_role_notes.educator: Always-on digital culture in HE is a structural issue; individual strategies alone are insufficient without policy support.
he_role_notes.student: Social media and always-online study cultures create specific wellbeing risks; student-facing resources need to address these directly.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Remote and hybrid working has amplified digital wellbeing issues; line managers play a key role.
he_role_notes.researcher: Research culture pressures interact with digital intensity in ways that require explicit acknowledgement.

ai_framing: AI tools can increase or decrease cognitive load depending on how they are used. Understanding this is part of intermediate-level digital wellbeing competence.

plain_language_summary: Understanding the environmental impact of digital technology use and making informed choices to reduce unnecessary consumption.
why_it_matters_in_he: HE institutions have sustainability commitments. Digital infrastructure has significant carbon footprint. Staff and students can influence this through informed choices.

basic.plain_description: Aware that digital technology has environmental impact.
basic.common_misread: Assumes environmental awareness equals behaviour change.
basic.example_in_he: A student learns that streaming video and large email attachments have a carbon footprint during a digital induction.

intermediate.plain_description: Makes informed choices to reduce digital environmental impact. Can explain the main sources of digital carbon footprint.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses digital with intangible -- assumes online equals carbon-free.
intermediate.example_in_he: A staff member compresses videos before uploading to the VLE, avoids printing unnecessarily, and uses energy-efficient settings on their devices.

advanced.plain_description: Evaluates digital systems or projects for environmental impact. Advocates for sustainable digital practice in institutional decision-making.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes IT knowledge is the primary driver of advanced competence here.
advanced.example_in_he: A digital project manager includes environmental impact criteria in the evaluation of new digital tools and advocates for carbon-aware procurement.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional digital sustainability strategy. Leads research or practice on green computing in HE.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates general sustainability leadership with digital sustainability expertise.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A sustainability director develops a digital carbon reduction roadmap covering infrastructure, user behaviour, and procurement.

he_role_notes.educator: Embedding digital sustainability in teaching is increasingly expected as part of education for sustainable development.
he_role_notes.student: Sustainability in digital practice is an employability-relevant attribute in many sectors.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Procurement and estates roles have the highest leverage on institutional digital environmental impact.
he_role_notes.researcher: Computationally intensive research (AI, simulation, genomics) has significant and often underacknowledged environmental costs.

ai_framing: Training and running large AI models is extremely energy-intensive. Understanding this cost is part of advanced digital sustainability competence, and relevant to responsible AI use decisions in HE.

plain_language_summary: Diagnosing and fixing technical issues with digital devices, software, and connectivity through systematic troubleshooting.
why_it_matters_in_he: Technical problems disrupt teaching, research, and professional work. A degree of autonomous problem-solving reduces dependency on IT support and keeps work moving.

basic.plain_description: Can apply simple fixes (restart, check connection, search for error message) before escalating.
basic.common_misread: Assumes heavy IT support users lack basic competence.
basic.example_in_he: A student troubleshoots a VLE login issue by clearing their browser cache and checking their password before contacting IT.

intermediate.plain_description: Diagnoses and resolves moderately complex technical issues independently. Knows when and how to escalate effectively.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses enthusiasm for tinkering with systematic troubleshooting competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer resolves an audio sync issue in a recorded lecture by identifying the codec problem and re-exporting with correct settings.

advanced.plain_description: Solves complex technical problems across systems. Designs diagnostic processes and supports others in troubleshooting.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes IT background is required for advanced competence.
advanced.example_in_he: A digital learning technologist diagnoses and resolves cross-browser compatibility issues in a custom VLE tool, documenting the solution for colleagues.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Leads technical problem-solving at institutional or sector level. Develops diagnostic frameworks or contributes to known-error databases.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates technical depth with organisational problem-solving leadership.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: An IT architecture lead develops a systematic approach to diagnosing performance issues across the university's digital infrastructure.

he_role_notes.educator: Sufficient technical problem-solving competence to continue teaching through minor technical failure is a practical expectation in digital teaching environments.
he_role_notes.student: Students often have high technical confidence but low systematic troubleshooting skill; direct instruction is effective.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Frontline service roles benefit from intermediate troubleshooting to reduce IT support dependency.
he_role_notes.researcher: Research computing issues (environment dependencies, package conflicts, HPC job failures) require intermediate-to-advanced troubleshooting.

ai_framing: AI assistants (Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT) are increasingly used for technical troubleshooting. Evaluating AI-suggested fixes critically before applying them is part of intermediate-level competence.

plain_language_summary: Recognising when a digital tool or approach could solve a problem, and selecting or evaluating the right technology for the right purpose.
why_it_matters_in_he: HE is awash with EdTech and digital tools. The ability to match need to tool -- or recognise when no tool is needed -- is essential for avoiding waste and delivering value.

basic.plain_description: Identifies familiar digital tools for common tasks.
basic.common_misread: Assumes knowing a wide range of tools equals competence in identifying the right one.
basic.example_in_he: A student identifies that a shared Google Doc is better than email chains for group writing.

intermediate.plain_description: Evaluates digital tools against defined criteria. Understands that the best tool depends on context, not just features.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses tool enthusiasm with needs analysis competence.
intermediate.example_in_he: A module team evaluates three VLE quiz tools against pedagogic, accessibility, and data requirements before selecting one.

advanced.plain_description: Designs technology selection processes for institutional or project use. Balances technical, pedagogic, ethical, and commercial considerations.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes technical evaluation is the primary component of tool selection.
advanced.example_in_he: A digital strategy manager leads a structured evaluation of AI writing tools for student use, including ethical risk assessment and academic integrity implications.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional frameworks for technology evaluation and procurement. Influences sector-level thinking on EdTech selection.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates procurement experience with strategic technology needs assessment.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A CIO develops a technology governance framework that embeds ethical evaluation, value assessment, and post-implementation review into all digital acquisitions.

he_role_notes.educator: Pedagogic need should drive tool selection, not the reverse; this is a common area of weakness in EdTech adoption.
he_role_notes.student: Tool selection for study and research projects is an increasingly important academic competence.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Procurement and project roles require systematic tool evaluation skills.
he_role_notes.researcher: Research tool selection has implications for reproducibility, data sovereignty, and ethical compliance.

ai_framing: The current proliferation of AI tools makes needs-based evaluation especially critical. Feature richness in AI tools can mask poor fit for specific HE contexts.

plain_language_summary: Using digital tools in novel, innovative, or imaginative ways to address challenges, create new knowledge, or enhance practice.
why_it_matters_in_he: Innovation in teaching, research, and professional services increasingly depends on creative application of digital technologies. This goes beyond using tools as designed.

basic.plain_description: Uses digital tools in new ways beyond their primary purpose when prompted.
basic.common_misread: Assumes frequent tool use leads naturally to creative application.
basic.example_in_he: A student uses a presentation tool to create a revision timeline after seeing a peer do so.

intermediate.plain_description: Independently experiments with digital tools to find creative solutions. Adapts tools to new contexts.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses creative use with technical novelty.
intermediate.example_in_he: A lecturer uses a collaborative whiteboard tool to facilitate a live peer feedback session in a way the tool was not originally designed for.

advanced.plain_description: Develops innovative digital approaches to teaching, research, or professional challenges. Shares and disseminates creative practice.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes innovation requires large budgets or specialist technical skills.
advanced.example_in_he: An educational developer designs a novel AI-augmented feedback workflow that significantly reduces marking time while improving feedback quality, and shares it across the institution.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Leads digital innovation initiatives. Builds capacity for creative digital practice across teams or institutions.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates innovation leadership with individual creative competence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A Head of Digital Innovation leads an experimentation programme that systematically surfaces, tests, and scales creative digital practices across the university.

he_role_notes.educator: Pedagogic creativity with digital tools distinguishes transformative from merely efficient teaching.
he_role_notes.student: Creative digital problem-solving is a valued graduate attribute across many sectors.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Process innovation through creative digital tool use can significantly improve efficiency.
he_role_notes.researcher: Methodological innovation in research increasingly involves creative use of digital and computational tools.

ai_framing: Generative AI opens up new creative possibilities but also introduces risks of surface-level novelty without depth. Creative use of AI in HE requires both imagination and critical evaluation.

plain_language_summary: Recognising what you do not yet know or cannot yet do digitally, and taking active steps to address those gaps through learning or collaboration.
why_it_matters_in_he: The digital landscape changes rapidly. The ability to self-assess and learn is more durable than any specific technical skill. In HE, it also supports effective CPD planning and team capability development.

basic.plain_description: Recognises when they lack a digital skill and is willing to seek help.
basic.common_misread: Assumes willingness to learn equals active gap identification.
basic.example_in_he: A student recognises they do not know how to use referencing software and completes a library workshop.

intermediate.plain_description: Accurately self-assesses digital competence, identifies specific gaps, and selects appropriate learning resources or peer support.
intermediate.common_misread: Confuses completing CPD activities with accurate self-assessment.
intermediate.example_in_he: A member of staff uses a digital skills self-assessment tool, identifies gaps in data management, and builds a personal development plan.

advanced.plain_description: Supports others in identifying and addressing digital competence gaps. Designs assessment tools or learning pathways for teams or cohorts.
advanced.common_misread: Assumes L&D experience equals digital competence gap analysis expertise.
advanced.example_in_he: A digital learning lead designs a team-level digital skills audit and uses the results to commission targeted training across a professional services department.

highly_advanced.plain_description: Develops institutional frameworks for digital competence assessment and development. Contributes to national or sector-level thinking on digital skills needs.
highly_advanced.common_misread: Conflates framework authorship with operational skills development competence.
highly_advanced.example_in_he: A Head of Digital Innovation leads the design of an institution-wide digital capability framework, assessment tool, and development programme aligned to strategic priorities.

he_role_notes.educator: Self-assessment of digital competence is a prerequisite for effective CPD; institutional frameworks can support but cannot replace individual agency.
he_role_notes.student: Students who can accurately self-assess their digital skills are better prepared for graduate employment.
he_role_notes.professional_services: Performance review processes that include digital competence discussion require at least intermediate self-assessment capability.
he_role_notes.researcher: Rapidly evolving research tools mean ongoing gap identification is a professional expectation.

ai_framing: AI tools can support competence gap identification (e.g. AI-assisted coaching or diagnostic tools) but cannot replace accurate self-knowledge. Overreliance on AI for self-assessment is itself a gap.
